- 99% accuracy recovery or better
- 5X smaller models
- 3X faster inference than the baseline.
How it works:
1️⃣ Start by sparsifying a model using LLM Compressor ( or choose a sparse foundation model from RedHat AI on Hugging Face, such as Sparse-Llama-3.1-8B-2of4 ( You can also bring your own sparse model, as long as it’s compatible with @huggingface transformers.

3️⃣ Finally, apply post-training quantization ( using LLM Compressor to compress the model further.

title: Casper Hansen (@casper_hansen_)
summary:
Recipe to post-train o3 into a DeepResearch model:
- Open-domain data that does not have an easily verifiable metric for success
- A search engine (could literally be anything, like your own vector search or whatever you fancy)
- LLM as a judge: your reward just becomes whatever the judge says (yes literally just this).
Two pieces of evidence:
- Noam Brown correctly claims DeepResearch does not have an easily verifiable metric for success, yet DeepResearch models exist so there must be some verification metric. (
- Kimi-Researcher claim they used the system prompt from Humanity's Last Exam with o3-mini to judge correctness on the open domain questions.(
How researchers got hardstuck on DeepSeek R1
The R1 paper specifically claims judges may lead to reward hacking. Everyone, myself included, interpreted this differently than how we should have.
The real interpretation is: when your problem is easily verifiable (code, math, multiple-choice), using a generative model is a dumb idea because you have much more accurate ways to measure success.
On a final note, don't get hard-stuck on just using judges. Mix in coding and math data for generalization.

title: Casper Hansen (@casper_hansen_)
summary:
Let me clarify the criticism: you generate 16 responses (16x tokens) and compare that to 1 response. Why not take Devstral and apply your Best@K?
Quoting @Agentica_
It's easy to confuse Best@K vs Pass@K—and we've seen some misconceptions about our results.
Our 59% on SWEBench-Verified is Pass@1 with Best@16, not Pass@8/16. Our Pass@8/16 is 67%/71%.
So how did we achieve this?
DeepSWE generates N candidate solutions. Then, another LLM (DeepSWE-Verifier) picks the best one to submit for evaluation. This is a classic form of test-time scaling (TTS) using Best@N.
Evaluating agents with TTS is common in SWEBench because there's no canonical agent design (unlike math or reasoning). Many top agents use multi-agent setups or agentic workflows (like Agentless), which naturally involve more LLM calls and test-time compute.
SWEBench ranks models by Pass@1, regardless of how many candidates were generated—as long as only one final solution is verified.
Among open-weight models, the top prior entry was Skywork-32B-SWE + TTS (Best@8) at 47%. DeepSWE + TTS (Best@16) now leads with 59% and becomes SOTA in this category.
Figure below shows how DeepSWE's performance scale with TTS:

title: Casper Hansen (@casper_hansen_)
summary:
A path to achieve DeepResearch models:
A great number of people believe we can use Knowledge Graphs to get to a great Deep Research model, potentially better than the current state of the art.
KGs allow you to represent and connect data in an intuitive way. You can hop from node to node, assess the situation and connected nodes at every step.
Reward functions for knowledge graphs
Assume we have a graph where each edge is assigned a weight. When you query the graph, you land at a specific point within the knowledge graph. From there, you can explore your way to the right answer.
There are multiple correct paths in such a graph, making the reward function super simple: what is the shortest path to the answer?
This gets more complicated for Deep Research as answers are open-ended. You have to figure out a way to answer: will the information in this node contribute to a correct answer? LLM as a judge could be a way to achieve this.
Benchmarks for knowledge graphs
Neo4J published a benchmark that is still unsolved today even though it's a toy example about connecting People based on Location, Gender, Marriage.
GPT-4o gets 1% on the Exact Match and o3 gets 4%. I helped some researchers eval against this Text2Cypher on their RL'd model which gets 12%.
Despite these improvements, graphs are largely an unsolved problem which multi-turn RL has a ton of potential to tap into. You can boostrap this eval into RL training data and a reward system.
Graphs today remind me much of when SWE-Bench was published in 2023. Everyone tried hard to ace it and Devin scoring 13.86% felt like a breakthrough at the time.

title: Casper Hansen (@casper_hansen_)
summary:
Qwen Lab released a DeepResearch Eval:
WebWalker: Benchmarking LLMs in Web Traversal.
Benchmarks nowadays are topped out on the S-curve
But this one is different!
o4-mini - 6.1% accuracy (33.0% on GAIA)
Qwen 2.5 72B agent - 12.0% accuracy (55.4% on GAIA)
OAI DeepResearch - 51.5% accuracy (67.4% on GAIA)
Let's explore:
1. Why this is a graph problem?
2. How you build the graph?
3. Why graphs are actually an RL problem
4. Rewards for graphs with RL
5. Multi-turn RL for knowledge graphs
Main difference between WebWalker and GAIA?
They are not entirely correlated. GAIA also appears outdated as a DeepResearch eval.
To be good at this benchmark: Traverse multiple web pages and synthesize an answer.
The graph problem
A lot of research and compute credits have been burned trying to solve LLMs + graphs.
Sadly, the truth is that information-seeking problems are graph traversal problems.
When DeepResearch scourers the internet, that's equivalent to building an information graph dynamically.
But this is not the right way for scientific problems. If you want to solve for biology or chemistry, you need a graph that is built in advance and which makes information discovery and association easy.
So how do you build the graph, anyway?
You start by deciding what information each node should contain and, crucially, what causal relationships the edges will represent.
One way to approach the problem is to build on a set of ontologies - a set of IDs that identify biologically important chemicals, genes, proteins, or pathways.
These become your nodes.
Now you need to establish the causal connections. Rather than simply linking papers to ontologies, you extract causal relationships from the literature.
Which entity upregulates, downregulates, or otherwise causally influences another? Those are your connections in the graph.
How graphs become RL problems
Each directed edge represents a causal relationship, with weights quantifying the strength of that influence.
But how do you build those weights?
You might find that Gene A strongly upregulates Protein B (positive weight), while Compound C moderately inhibits Pathway D (negative weight).
A simple approach: Weak=0.2, moderate=0.5, strong=0.8. If downregulated, just do -weight. Then the cost becomes 1/abs(weight).
(note: this more complicated than it sounds and needs to be thoughtfully determined)
There we go. A graph with costs associated for actions.
RL training rewards for exploration
What if your model could learn to reduce the actions needed to answer a question from 200 -> 20 just by properly rewarding it?
What we just discussed is an efficiency reward, potentially reducing a 50 minute problem to a 5 minute problem.
The trifecta of RL here is going to be format, efficiency, and accuracy. We just solved efficiency which is the main problem with graphs because they can span millions or billions or data points.
Aha moment for pathfinding
This is essentially a pathfinding algorithm. While largely unexplored, I would not be surprised if there is an "aha moment" of finding similar pathfinding abilities to Dijkstra's algorithm trained into the model.
Dijkstra’s algorithm efficiently finds shortest paths in weighted graphs by prioritizing low-cost edges
A well-trained RL policy should learn to navigate causal graphs similarly: prioritizing high-weight edges (strong causal links) and avoiding low-weight detours unless strictly necessary.
Multi-turn RL for Knowledge Graphs
Training a model with multi-turn RL from here is key. You have solved efficiency. Format is trivial, but you have not yet thought about accuracy.
Tool calling:
- The action space will be large in this case.
- You need tools that can query the graph by searching.
- Graph hop conditions, e.g. you are stuck in high-cost jumps that you are not confident about.
- Exit conditions for when you are done searching.
Rubric for Accuracy:
- Applying a judge with guiding principles is the easiest
- The judge can be a trained verifier or just an API model that you query during reward computation

title: Casper Hansen (@casper_hansen_)
summary:
Recipe to post-train DeepSeek V3 into a CUDA Optimization engine:
CUDA-L1 nets a 17.7x average speedup on KernelBench by using a three-stage approach including RL.
(Show the Candy Trail) Contrastive RL:
> Standard RL hides the reward from the model during reasoning.
> Teach the model to distinguish between faster and slower CUDA implementation.
> Do this by augmenting the prompt with code and rewards from previous epochs.
(Hack the Hackers) Reward hacking was dealt with by:
> Avoiding superficial speedups by artificially reducing original values like batch size and tensor dimensions
> Avoiding inflated speedup metrics by using cached results from previous execution
(Tiny Side-Eye) Minor critiques:
> Authors only avoid reward hacking by system prompting, could have introduced some rule-based constraints
> Train and eval data is the same, creating some bias in results although you would expect generalization as we have seen from prior research in RL
> Model and code is not published and GitHub repository is GPL licensed.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gwc5SDcXMAAsMn3.jpg

title: Casper Hansen (@casper_hansen_)
summary:
Recipe to post-train Qwen3 1.7B into a DeepResearch model
What does it mean for something small to think deeply? Meet Lucy, a post‑trained Qwen3‑1.7B as a DeepResearch model based on @willccbb's verifiers.
Primary Rule-based Rewards:
- Answer correctness
We check whether the final response literally contains the ground-truth answer. This substring match is cheap and avoids calling a larger LLM judge.
- Visit/search ratio
If the agent visits at least as many pages as it issues search queries, it receives ((visit_search_ratio - 1) / 4) ** 0.25. If it searches more than it visits, the score is -0.5.
Format / Anti Reward-Hacking Rewards:
- Tool execution success
Each API call that returns without an error counts. The reward is (successful_calls * unique_tools_used) / total_call_attempts.
- Thinking efficiency
A skew-normal penalty centered at 70 tokens discourages endless chain-of-thought between tool calling while still allowing enough tokens for planning.
This is how Qwen3 1.7B learned to search, visit, and synthesize information. Small models can do deep research too!

title: Casper Hansen (@casper_hansen_)
summary:
A quick lesson on efficiency in DeepResearch models
Think selectively, not deterministically
Quoting @alandao_ai
What happens if you reward shorter "thinking on average"?
We observed this in Lucy🍎 - the model will skip thinking.
How does this work?
Let's say you have a model that researches a topic in 5 turns, each is x_i:
x_1 - Search about the topic <think>
x_2 - Read the page from the search result <think>
x_3 - Read the page from the search result <think>
x_4 - Read the page from the search result <think>
x_5 - Search some other details <think>
-> Answer
Every time the model makes a tool call to search or read, it will perform a round of thinking.
But if you reward the model for being "more efficient" on average, it will naturally stop thinking in x_2, x_3, and x_4 , because the most efficient strategy is to read through the search results first, then start thinking.
It became:
x_1 - Search about the topic <think>
x_2 - Read the page from the search result <nothink>
x_3 - Read the page from the search result <nothink>
x_4 - Read the page from the search result <nothink>
x_5 - Search some other details <think>
-> Answer
As a result, steps 2, 3, and 4 become more efficient by having just 0 tokens inside the <think> tag.
Originally, we expected Lucy to reduce the average length of thinking, meaning each round of thinking would be shorter. Instead, the model learned to skip thinking entirely when it wasn't needed. This is much smarter because the model can reserve the test-time compute ability, yet be more efficient on obvious strategy like....reading the search results that you found before overthinking.
You can support Lucy at:
It's a 1.7B model with ability to do research, agentic search and run on mobile well enough!

summary:
Researchers designed a 27M model inspired by the brain. It outperforms o3-mini, R1, and others.
This makes every single AI lab look silly!
Here are their 5 core techniques:
- Brain-inspired hierarchical processing, temporal separation, and recurrent connectivity
- Hierarchical convergence: designed for stable convergence to avoid getting stuck like in RNNs
- Approximate gradient: designed to keep constant memory and avoids unrolling through time like in RNNs
- Deep supervision: sequential computation of states with retainment of final hidden states (conclusion of segment)
- Adaptive computational time: automatically switches between system 1 and 2 thinking by a halting mechanism. This uses deep supervision and Q-learning.

title: Casper Hansen (@casper_hansen_)
summary:
Announcing a NEW hard biology benchmark!
✨A little background of why I created this:
Progress in biological discovery is analogous to a needle-in-a-haystack problem over the entire evidence landscape.
Scientists are information weavers. They mine sparse signals over scattered research articles to form a scientific rationale. They identify what *might* work given the limited evidence.
The benchmarks available today for biology or medicine are largely saturated. A more fundamental problem is that biology is open-ended, which these benchmarks do not reflect with multiple-choice questions.
🎯 How this benchmark was created
To create this benchmark, there is a total of 7 steps over two phases.
To create the base dataset:
1. Download full research articles from PubMed Central, filter for domain specific to diabetes and obesity.
2. Create embeddings over each article and discard anything that exceeds 32k tokens (1% of data).
3. Create clusters of 6 research articles by creating a HNSW index and using ANN search. Measure average similarity of clusters and keep >0.75 (3.75% of data).
From this base dataset, an extensive pipeline is deployed to synthesise the final dataset by using DeepSeek R1:
1. Generate a question-answer pair that integrates information from the six provided research articles.
2. Score the pair on difficulty, askability, synthesizability, abstractiveness, and conflict synthesis. Discard any that fail the thresholds.
3. Retain the sample only if the model can answer it with the context but not without it, confirming both correctness and difficulty.
4. Split on difficulty. PhD becomes the test split, and graduate becomes the train split.
We end up with a dataset of 5.11k samples, 338 samples being for the benchmark.
🏹 State-of-the-art in biology
SOTA will be defined by agents capable of long-horizon tasks. Today, SOTA is o3's DeepResearch model which gets 31.7% accuracy. This proves that search with reasoning improves the score on this benchmark.
The top open-source models just about match o4-mini in performance with 1% difference (52 vs 57 correct samples). Meanwhile there is a much bigger gap of 8.3% difference in accuracy between o3 and open-source models.
For full transparency, the only model I evaluated which had search capabilities activated was DeepResearch as it's a costly endeavour. Additionally, DeepSeek R1 has been excluded from this benchmark for fairness since we adversarially constructed hard questions against the model.
Final dataset:
Code:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GxruhFmWwAAu13z.jpg

title: Casper Hansen (@casper_hansen_)
summary:
Zhipu AI released their GLM 4.5 paper! They train reasoning, agentic, and general experts, and then they mix them into one by distillation.
A few highlights:
Generalization:
- they trained their agentic model for web search and SWE tasks
- this leads to generalized performance improvements across other tasks and benchmarks, such as general tool usage and coding tasks like Terminal-Benc
Two-stage GRPO difficulty curriculum for reasoning:
- Stage 1: n=16 for moderate problems
- Stage 2: n=512 for extremely hard problems because pass@8-16 is likely always zero
Token-weighted loss for code RL:
- code RL converges faster with a token-weighted mean loss instead of sequence-mean, reducing length bias and suppressing trivial base-case outputs.
Temperature is adjusted dynamically during RL:
- when rollout rewards plateau they raise temperature to boost exploration
- increase up to the highest value that doesn't drop validation performance by >1%
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GyC9Fv4XAAU5LmJ.jpg

We measured token usage across reasoning models: open models output 1.5-4x more tokens than closed models on identical tasks, but with huge variance depending on task type (up to 10x on simple questions).

title: Casper Hansen (@casper_hansen_)
summary:
a system like this will probably survive yet be banished to irrelevance. a good blog post is better than a paper.
Quoting @redtachyon
It really feels like ICLR 2026 is a pivotal moment for the beginning of the collapse of the ML peer review system. Complaints about bad reviews and bad papers have always been around, but not nearly to this extent.
The annoying thing about the conference system is that to criticize it, you need to first be successful in it - else you're just a sore loser. I've had successes and failures in various conferences, some reasonable, some weird. I don't claim to be an authority, but I do claim to be passionate about the field and have a vested interest in its success.
Growing up as a lil' science nerd, I loved the idea of peer review - fellow respected scientists gathering to check whether a paper is legit, suggesting changes to make it better, working together in the pursuit of Science.
This, of course, is not the reality. I'm not old enough to make a diagnosis as for how and when it happened. But the cat is out of the bag, and we're stuck in this mess, at least until some respected scientist/organization proposes a new paradigm - either drastically more closed, or drastically more open.
The modern conference model is a randomized scarcity measure, and I really mean it. It's random - the NeurIPS consistency experiment shows that painfully clearly. It is also, by design, a scarcity tactic - conferences generally target a fixed percentage of accepted papers, also accounting for venue limits. Quality of the papers is secondary, and "good paper, reject" is a perfectly acceptable outcome.
The only thing that keeps this system alive is a vague vibe of prestige among some (fewer each day) researchers, and institutional lock-in by dinosaurs in academia.
Is there a better way? I don't know. I see two paths. Either (a) we move to a radically more open paradigm, where everyone puts their papers on neoarXiv, and everyone else can participate in some sort of voting/commentary system; or (b) a new, more elitist publishing system is established, where bad authors and bad reviewers are excluded. Note that this will also impact newcomers to the field - ever since having a paper in a top AI conference became a potential money generator, endless hordes of grifters started flooding our field, and it will only get worse. These people have to be excluded.
None of these paths are particularly good, but they're probably better than what we have now.
Sometimes I half-jokingly say that democratization of AI has gone too far, and we need to bring back gatekeeping. I sorta stand by that - but we need a way to distinguish well-meaning beginners from clout-driven grifters.
Unfortunately, the cultural zeitgeist still swings in the way of radical democratization - so any measures that might adversely impact those well-meaning beginners (who I absolutely want to support) will immediately get rejected by the more established and experienced people in the field.
It will get worse before it gets better. If it gets better.
Hopefully our superintelligent overlords arrive soon to fix this for us.

title: Casper Hansen (@casper_hansen_)
summary:
Agents today largely have the same dynamics as RL:
- you give it data (code/instruction) to complete a task
- you design a verification mechanism
- it executes, learns, and tries again in a loop
Karpathy: I do think it’s possible that in-context learning runs a small gradient descent loop internally in the layers of the neural network
If you have experience using Claude Code and designing verification mechanisms which it uses in a loop, you are halfway there to doing RL. The hardest part about RL is the infrastructure and stability.
Quoting @karpathy
My pleasure to come on Dwarkesh last week, I thought the questions and conversation were really good.
I re-watched the pod just now too. First of all, yes I know, and I'm sorry that I speak so fast :). It's to my detriment because sometimes my speaking thread out-executes my thinking thread, so I think I botched a few explanations due to that, and sometimes I was also nervous that I'm going too much on a tangent or too deep into something relatively spurious. Anyway, a few notes/pointers:
AGI timelines. My comments on AGI timelines looks to be the most trending part of the early response. This is the "decade of agents" is a reference to this earlier tweet Basically my AI timelines are about 5-10X pessimistic w.r.t. what you'll find in your neighborhood SF AI house party or on your twitter timeline, but still quite optimistic w.r.t. a rising tide of AI deniers and skeptics. The apparent conflict is not: imo we simultaneously 1) saw a huge amount of progress in recent years with LLMs while 2) there is still a lot of work remaining (grunt work, integration work, sensors and actuators to the physical world, societal work, safety and security work (jailbreaks, poisoning, etc.)) and also research to get done before we have an entity that you'd prefer to hire over a person for an arbitrary job in the world. I think that overall, 10 years should otherwise be a very bullish timeline for AGI, it's only in contrast to present hype that it doesn't feel that way.
Animals vs Ghosts. My earlier writeup on Sutton's podcast . I am suspicious that there is a single simple algorithm you can let loose on the world and it learns everything from scratch. If someone builds such a thing, I will be wrong and it will be the most incredible breakthrough in AI. In my mind, animals are not an example of this at all - they are prepackaged with a ton of intelligence by evolution and the learning they do is quite minimal overall (example: Zebra at birth). Putting our engineering hats on, we're not going to redo evolution. But with LLMs we have stumbled by an alternative approach to "prepackage" a ton of intelligence in a neural network - not by evolution, but by predicting the next token over the internet. This approach leads to a different kind of entity in the intelligence space. Distinct from animals, more like ghosts or spirits. But we can (and should) make them more animal like over time and in some ways that's what a lot of frontier work is about.
On RL. I've critiqued RL a few times already, e.g. . First, you're "sucking supervision through a straw", so I think the signal/flop is very bad. RL is also very noisy because a completion might have lots of errors that might get encourages (if you happen to stumble to the right answer), and conversely brilliant insight tokens that might get discouraged (if you happen to screw up later). Process supervision and LLM judges have issues too. I think we'll see alternative learning paradigms. I am long "agentic interaction" but short "reinforcement learning" I've seen a number of papers pop up recently that are imo barking up the right tree along the lines of what I called "system prompt learning" , but I think there is also a gap between ideas on arxiv and actual, at scale implementation at an LLM frontier lab that works in a general way. I am overall quite optimistic that we'll see good progress on this dimension of remaining work quite soon, and e.g. I'd even say ChatGPT memory and so on are primordial deployed examples of new learning paradigms.
Cognitive core. My earlier post on "cognitive core": , the idea of stripping down LLMs, of making it harder for them to memorize, or actively stripping away their memory, to make them better at generalization. Otherwise they lean too hard on what they've memorized. Humans can't memorize so easily, which now looks more like a feature than a bug by contrast. Maybe the inability to memorize is a kind of regularization. Also my post from a while back on how the trend in model size is "backwards" and why "the models have to first get larger before they can get smaller"
Time travel to Yann LeCun 1989. This is the post that I did a very hasty/bad job of describing on the pod: . Basically - how much could you improve Yann LeCun's results with the knowledge of 33 years of algorithmic progress? How constrained were the results by each of algorithms, data, and compute? Case study there of.
nanochat. My end-to-end implementation of the ChatGPT training/inference pipeline (the bare essentials)
On LLM agents. My critique of the industry is more in overshooting the tooling w.r.t. present capability. I live in what I view as an intermediate world where I want to collaborate with LLMs and where our pros/cons are matched up. The industry lives in a future where fully autonomous entities collaborate in parallel to write all the code and humans are useless. For example, I don't want an Agent that goes off for 20 minutes and comes back with 1,000 lines of code. I certainly don't feel ready to supervise a team of 10 of them. I'd like to go in chunks that I can keep in my head, where an LLM explains the code that it is writing. I'd like it to prove to me that what it did is correct, I want it to pull the API docs and show me that it used things correctly. I want it to make fewer assumptions and ask/collaborate with me when not sure about something. I want to learn along the way and become better as a programmer, not just get served mountains of code that I'm told works. I just think the tools should be more realistic w.r.t. their capability and how they fit into the industry today, and I fear that if this isn't done well we might end up with mountains of slop accumulating across software, and an increase in vulnerabilities, security breaches and etc.
Job automation. How the radiologists are doing great and what jobs are more susceptible to automation and why.
Physics. Children should learn physics in early education not because they go on to do physics, but because it is the subject that best boots up a brain. Physicists are the intellectual embryonic stem cell I have a longer post that has been half-written in my drafts for ~year, which I hope to finish soon.
Thanks again Dwarkesh for having me over!

title: Casper Hansen (@casper_hansen_)
summary:
Cohere using AWQ! Quantization is one of the strongest tradeoffs you can make with very little loss but huge memory savings for on-prem/private models
Quoting @RedHat_AI
Cohere shared a strong production case study during recent @vllm_project office hours on how they use LLM Compressor and the AWQ compression algorithm to make large MoE models deployable.
Their focus is private, on-prem deployments where GPUs and cost are tightly constrained. Many Cohere models use Mixture-of-Experts architectures, which significantly increases inference-time memory. Without 4-bit weight quantization, these models would be impractical to deploy.
LLM Compressor enables fast exploration of quantization strategies through adaptable algorithms, non-uniform quantization across layers, and seamless integration with vLLM for rapid iteration.
A key challenge was calibration. Using standard datasets degraded performance on long-context agentic tasks inside North, Cohere's enterprise AI platform. Analysis showed failures were driven by repetitive chat templates and tool descriptions biasing AWQ statistics.
By adding token masking support to AWQ in LLM Compressor, Cohere eliminated that bias and produced production-ready 4-bit models that met their quality bar.
As hardware evolved, Cohere extended AWQ from INT4 W4A16 to NVFP4 W4A16 for Blackwell GPUs, and observed meaningful speedups with W4A8 for compute-bound workloads. Dense and MoE W4A8 serving is supported in vLLM today.
This is a great example of why LLM Compressor matters for real systems, not just benchmarks.
Huge thanks to Zewen Shen, Ali Edalati, Bharat Venkitesh, and the team at @cohere for sharing this work, and to the @RedHat AI team for their hard work on making LLM Compressor a production-grade model optimization library.
P.S. Both Cohere and Red Hat are hiring! If you want to work on efficient AI, reply to this post and we'll get in touch.

title: Casper Hansen (@casper_hansen_)
summary:
quick breakdown of the RL infrastructure at play:
algorithm
> uses grpo with double-sided token-level masking
> based on probability ratio between the training policy and inference policy for each generated token
long-tail samples
> fp8 to reduce inter-token latency
> multi-token prediction with accept length of 2.76
> data parallel aware routing to maximize KV-cache reuse
> prefill-decode disaggregation to avoid prefill disrupting progress of decode
agentic RL
> fully async RL
> batch is sent to the training engine to update the model based on threshold of number of samples
> weight updates at every K steps along with resetting optimizer
> discard a sample if its oldest rollout version is too stale based on τ threshold
> discard a sample if the coding-agent sandboxes fail due to environment crashing
> token-in token-out is a key part of the training, eliminating mismatches between inference and training
reward system
> a mix of rule-based, outcome models, and generative models to measure 3 objectives:
> foundational correctness: accurate, logically sound, and fully follows the user’s instructions
> emotional intelligence: adds empathy, insight, and a natural tone
> task-specific quality: refines each response to excel within its particular domain
Quoting @Zai_org
Presenting the GLM-5 Technical Report!
After the launch of GLM-5, we’re pulling back the curtain on how it was built. Key innovations include:
- DSA Adoption: Significantly reduces training and inference costs while preserving long-context fidelity
- Asynchronous RL Infrastructure: Drastically improves post-training efficiency by decoupling generation from training
- Agent RL Algorithms: Enables the model to learn from complex, long-horizon interactions more effectively
Through these innovations, GLM-5 achieves SOTA performance among open-source models, with particularly strong results in real-world software engineering tasks.

title: Casper Hansen (@casper_hansen_)
clean_title: Reproducing Project Glasswing with Clearwing's open-source workflow
summary:
Eric reproduced the Glasswing project in record time. Mythos is good but the vulnerabilities come from the workflow in the agent harness
Quoting @QuixiAI
Last week, Anthropic announced Project Glasswing alongside Claude Mythos Preview, a model they described as so powerful at finding vulnerabilities they couldn't release it. The announcement featured AWS, Microsoft, Google, and Apple as partners, $100M in compute credits, and a clear message: this is dangerous, and only we can be trusted to deploy it safely.
The results were real. Thousands of zero-days across every major OS and browser. A 27-year-old bug in OpenBSD. A 16-year-old bug in FFmpeg. Fully autonomous exploit chains that would have taken human researchers weeks.
But here's what bothered me: all the credit went to the model.
Read the technical blog carefully and a different picture emerges. The real innovation isn't the model. It's the workflow:
- Rank every file in a codebase by attack surface
- Fan out hundreds of parallel agents, each scoped to one file
- Use crash oracles (AddressSanitizer, UBSan) as ground truth
- Run a second verification agent to filter noise
- Generate exploits as a triage mechanism for severity
That's a pipeline. And pipelines are model-agnostic.
At Lazarus AI, we spend our days deploying custom AI in places where "just use the closed API" isn't an option: regulated industries, enterprise, and government. When I saw Glasswing, my instinct was the same one I have every week: strip out the proprietary model, keep the architecture, run it on whatever model is best for the customer.
Clearwing is a fully open-source vulnerability discovery engine. Crash-first hunting, file-parallel agents, oracle-driven verification, variant hunting, adversarial verification. Works with any LLM.
I tested it with OpenAI Codex 5.4 and reproduced Glasswing's findings. I'm now reproducing results with our own ReAligned model - Qwen3.5 finetuned to Western alignment.
Mythos is certainly a great model. The N-day exploit walkthroughs in Anthropic's blog show real reasoning depth. But it's an incremental improvement over Opus, the same way Opus was over Sonnet, and Sonnet over Haiku. It's not a leap to superintelligence. It's the next point on a curve we've been watching for years.
What actually changed the game was the workflow.
Defenders shouldn't have to wait for access to a gated model to secure their software. These vulnerabilities have been sitting in codebases for decades. The tools to find them should be available to everyone: the open source maintainer running FFmpeg on a Saturday, the startup that can't afford $125/M output tokens, the researcher in a country where Anthropic doesn't operate.
Clearwing is MIT licensed and available now.
Clearwing enables a wide variety of security activities. Handle with care. It is sharp.

clean_title: Anticipating DeepSeek V4 and its performance implications
summary:
There was a time around DeepSeek R1 where there was no conceivable gap in my experience. I wonder if we will see the same with DeepSeek V4 coming soon?
Any whale watchers that can make early conclusions based on the model deployed on DeepSeek Chat?
Quoting @natolambert
I've been trying to grapple with what the key inputs are to the open-closed performance gap, and how they're changing.
Until the training paradigm changes, open weight models will pretty clearly be able to fast-follow closed labs. There are sources of uncertainty, but that fact of keeping up seems hard to shake. I spent a long time looking for evidence of or arguments supporting open models falling behind, but it's not there at all today.
Things I consider include:
- How benchmarks evolve over time, becoming more or less correlated with how people actually use models,
- How different models’ real-world performance relates to their benchmark rankings, and
- How training regimes evolve over time to move said benchmarks.
I roughly conclude that this equilibrium will last until economic forces initiate a change in strategy, or training needs shift.
An example I'm wondering is if closed models more directly integrate user training data, which open labs cannot access, they could pull ahead.

title: Casper Hansen (@casper_hansen_)
clean_title: Token-In, Token-Out: Fixing Fragile Tokenization in Agent Loops
summary:
Tokenization is fragile, especially in agent loops. Do the correct thing and focus on append-only, token-in token-out. This will save you countless times from silently wrong training runs.
Quoting @ClementDelangue
Most people training agentic LLMs with RL right now have a silently broken training loop and have no idea.
Here's the trap: single-turn RL works beautifully. Clean curves, sane rewards, everything converges. Then you add tools so the model can act mid-rollout, and things get weird. Loss spikes for no reason. Eventually a shape-mismatch error.
The culprit: every time you parse the model's output to detect a tool call, then re-tokenize the updated conversation for the next turn, you're rolling the dice. Usually the round-trip gives back the same tokens. Sometimes it doesn't and your gradient lands on a sequence the model never actually sampled. No crash. Just quietly wrong math and a useless gradient signal.
The fix is one rule: never re-encode tokens you've decoded. Keep the sampled tokens in one buffer, never re-render them, and both failure modes disappear. That's Token-In, Token-Out done right.
Our team just published a beautiful deep-dive on exactly this, including an audit across the major open-weights model families showing most chat templates already support it. Required reading if you're doing multi-turn RL 🤗🔥
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJc2cXRWsAMbdXD.jpg
clean_summary:
Tokenization is fragile, especially in agent loops. The key is to focus on append-only, token-in token-out processing, which prevents silent errors during training.

Most current training loops for agentic LLMs with reinforcement learning have a hidden flaw. When the model's output is parsed to call tools and then re-tokenized for the next turn, sometimes the re-tokenization changes the tokens. This mismatch can lead to incorrect gradients without any obvious errors, causing silent training failures.

The solution is simple: never re-encode tokens that have already been decoded. Keep the sampled tokens in a buffer and avoid re-rendering them, ensuring consistent token sequences. A recent deep-dive and audit across major open-weight models show that most chat templates already support this approach, making multi-turn RL more reliable and effective.

@haoailab introduces JetSpec, a method that uses speculative decoding with causal parallel tree drafting to significantly reduce LLM generation latency. JetSpec achieves up to 9.64 times speedup on MATH-500 and 4.58 times on open-ended chat while maintaining lossless quality. linked_urls.title: JetSpec: Breaking the Scaling Ceiling of Speculative Decoding with Parallel Tree Drafting | Hao AI Lab @ UCSD
linked_urls.summary: TL;DR: Speculative decoding hits a scaling ceiling: a larger draft budget helps only while acceptance stays high and drafting stays cheap. Prior draft heads face a dilemma: autoregressive drafters condition on each path but pay with tree depth, while block-diffusion drafters draft in one pass but score branches independently, creating plausible yet mutually inconsistent trees. JetSpec trains a causal parallel draft head over fused hidden states from a frozen target model, so candidate-tree scores follow the target’s own autoregressive factorization.

clean_summary: Casper Hansen suggests that in about six months, people will realize they are no longer distilling models, noting that the main difference now is open access to decide how weights are distributed. He also mentions that the yolo-run was likely not very cheap. A quoted reply from @oguzerkan counters this, stating that Chinese companies are not building state-of-the-art models by investing a fraction of what US companies do. Instead, they are distilling US models, combining US capital expenditure with their own, and not doing anything that researchers in the Valley cannot solve.
